The Third Conditional

There are four types of conditional sentences in English:
  1. Zero Conditional - to talk about certainty and facts
  2. First Conditional - to talk about real possibilities in the present or the future
  3. Second Conditional - to talk about unreal possibilities in the present or the future
  4. Third Conditional - to talk about unreal past situations

You use third conditional to talk about unreal situations in the past.
These are things that did not happen in the past. You often use the third conditional to talk about regrets.

If Corbin had offered me a job I probably would have taken it.
If Durban Inc. had been interested, I would have probably gone there.
Lisa would have gone to Turbo Store, if they had given her a better deal, but they didn't.
I am glad they didn't because I wouldn't have found my new partner if she had joined that firm.
The Future Continuous Tense vs. The Future Perfect Tense

You use the Future Continuous tense to talk about something happening at a particular time in the future.
You use the Future Perfect tense to talk about an action in the future before another action in the future. This is the past in the future.
When you use the Future Continuous tense, the action will have started before that moment but it will not have finished at that moment.

For example:
I will be working at 4 p.m. tomorrow.
The person will start work at some point in the future and be working at 4 p.m. It is not clear when the person will stop working.

The structure of the Future Continuous is:
Subject + will + be + verb -ing
In six months, our website will be up and operating.
You can sometimes think of the Future Perfect tense like the Present Perfect tense, but instead of your viewpoint being in the present, it is in the future.

For example:
You can call me at work at 8 a.m. I will have arrived at the office by 8.
The train will leave the station at 9 a.m. You will arrive at the station at 9:15 a.m. When you arrive, the train will have left.

The structure of the Future Perfect tense is:
Subject + will + (not) have + past participle
We will have designed the website and created some curriculum.
*Notice the position of not. It comes between will and have.
In six months, our website will be up and operating.
We will have designed the website and created some curriculum.
We will have moved into an office and we will have hired a staff.
At the end of a year, we hope we will be selling our curriculum to schools around the world.

Well, it has been a long few months, hasn't it?
I said I would have a job after four months and I am happy and excited to report that I do. My friend Lisa and I are opening our own online education website. But you were going to work at Corbin, weren't you? Well, if Corbin had offered me a job I probably would have taken it, and if Durban Inc. had been interested, I would have probably gone there. Lisa would have gone to Turbo Store, if they had given her a better deal, but they didn't. I am glad they didn't because I wouldn't have found my new partner if she had joined that firm.

Deep down we both had the same question that needed to be answered, “how to make education more accessible?”. We wanted to create something substantial and innovative that we both would be eager to dive into. Lisa has a top notch business mind and is always on the ball and I will be in charge of the technical side. We are going to keep things small at first because we shouldn't go too fast too soon, should we? So we have set some goals for ourselves. In six months, our website will be up and operating. We will have designed the website and created some curriculum. We will have moved into an office and we will have hired a staff.

At the end of a year, we hope we will be selling our curriculum to schools around the world.
We have finished, haven't we?
You will stay in touch, won't you?
